comments.name: Wanda Fewka
comments.body:
Leaving the discussion of details to others, here is a "big picture" observation: the Democrats need to return clearly and unequivocally to being the party that represents the interests of ordinary working people against the predations of an increasingly dominant and arrogant economic oligarchy. Their detour into primarily becoming a party espousing identity politics, whatever the individual merits of the various causes, has erroneously placed cultural identity issues at the forefront -- with disastrous consequences. 

So why did this happen? The simple answer is that, in response to the Reagan era and an increasing dominance of money in politics, party leaders decided that in order to compete effectively they needed more Wall Street support. And Wall Street money had its price -- reduced militancy against corporate interests. Support for the working class became little more than a ritual talking point, an empty symbolic nod.

And quiet betrayal produced guilt. And guilt produced an overcompensation. Secondary identity issues assumed a magnified importance, evolving into an ideological litmus test. Democrats no longer needed to devote themselves to the hard work of representing the working class against a powerful oligarchy. Identity politics was not only purer but also easier.

And identity politics finessed a second sticky problem -- the tension between unions and environmentalists. Environmental protection eliminated jobs. Identity politics made that conflict manageable.

While there was tough early rhetoric about crippling Iran’s military capabilities, the nuclear red line has remained the central focus. The piece does a reasonable job describing the current military stalemate, but it subtly pushes a “Trump is backing down” narrative instead of acknowledging the consistency of his stated goals.

I've had other friends say the same thing happened with their relatives that were dying.

comments.name: Matthew
comments.body:
Great article. 
My grandfather was in his final days in hospice, in a coma. I travelled to pay him my last respects. Sitting at the bed, my grandmother said "Matthew is here, honey" and he sat bolt upright, asking "Matthew?" He couldn't see me, but he remained sitting, we held hands, and we spoke normally together for about 15-20 minutes until he got too tired or the stress was too much. He hadn't responded to any oral stimuli in months, and never did again, dying a couple of weeks afterwards. My grandmother and the staff said it was a miracle. We got to say goodbye. It has meant so much to me, personally, and I will never again underestimate what those in a coma perceive about the world around them.

comments.name: MaryR
comments.body: My mom was sent home for hospice for congestive heart failure. The first week home, she was still very lucid. She held court for all her children and extended family who came to pay homage to the matriarch of the large family. She declined the second week until  she seemed unaware of her surroundings. She kept on in that state for several days until the last of her seven children was able to make it from Germany. She couldn't speak by then, but she looked at him and squeezed his hand. Shortly after, she died. The hospice nurse says she often sees patients hang on remarkably until a loved one visits and then die.

comments.name: HE
comments.body: My father had Alzheimer’s and ultimately never recognized me or my mother. We took turns spending alternating entire days with him at his care facility in the last months of his life. I would shave him regularly and cut his hair and he would smile and say “thank you, miss”.  One day it was my mother’s turn to visit. He was in a wheelchair in the hallway when she arrive and he turned to her and beamed “0h, Lusia, my beautiful wife, I love you so much “ in his native Polish. He died within a week, but left that memory as a precious gift to us.

He suffered with paranoia and sleeplessness which made caregiving extremely difficult.  Interestingly enough he also had moments of lucidity when everything came back to him and he knew the fate he was suffering and said it was like being trapped in his body in this horrible state.  He even asked his children to help him end his life and this terrible suffering during one such moment of lucidity.  It was heartbreaking.

comments.name: George Witte

comments.name: Michael McColly
comments.body: My mother suffered from Alzheimers for many years, and toward the end of her life, she, too, had moments of lucidity that startled me, my sisters and her care-workers. Speech had disappeared when she lost her mobility. She curled in her bed or in her uncomfortable wheel chair. But when, I moved to help my sisters and began to visit her regularly, spending time in her facility, she changed. Out of the blue, came complete sentences again, questions, like "what are these little machines everyone has?" She once asked, referring to cell phones. "I want one." She said looking directly into my eyes. Sometimes she would respond to the tone of my voice,   or if I sighed, she would automatically ask: "What is wrong, honey?"  I attribute these moments of clarity to emotional memory. Feeling our presence, feeling our touch, hearing our voices, my mother's emotional memory was triggered and out of the fog of her brain came these lucid responses of touch and speech. The emotional brain is mysterious and complex indeed and lies deep within.

I would suggest that the key factor in America rejecting the so-called "American left" is the degree to which leftism was hijacked by the Port Huron/"university students are the future" approach post-1968. The country has been debating this alienating, urban-focused, academic-based vision of avant-garde social justice and identity politics for almost 60 years and it has proven to be an electoral loser for most Dems going back to the 70s.

The turn occurred in earnest with the wave of college campus "occupations" in protest of the Vietnam War, a cause that had its merits, but failed to carry the minds of American voters in the way civil rights did. The shift to higher education as a center of political change reinforced for many the elitism and irrelevance of leftist political reforms, in part because college students could evade the draft. The increasing dominance of leftism in social sciences and humanities made things worse as faculty became the sources of many radical ideas that emerged in the later 60s and 70s. The close relationship between urban locales and higher education concentrated support for these ideas in non-rural areas, ceding the field to conservatives.

Democrats are still living down this toxic legacy. The Gaza encampments, for example, were the perfect opportunity for Republicans to remind voters of the obnoxious protests of the 60s that Reagan rode to victory on in his race for governor. Democrats need to fix this problem, now.

Both politicians and the media have falsely ascribed political motivation to the judges and justices of our judiciary. 

Most judges and justices believe it is their job to apply the law and the Constitution, and do their best to do so. Judges do render their judicial evaluations influenced to some degree by their own political perspectives. But, with some unfortunate exceptions, they are trying to honor our laws and our Constitution, and not define policy. Setting policy is the job of Congress and the Executive branch; members of the judiciary know this, and try to do their jobs as best they can.

It is unfortunate that many politicians and media pundits have undermined our courts by denying this separation of powers. President Biden was one of the most egregious offenders, when he falsely claimed the Dobbs decision was an “exercise in raw political power.”  It was not; rather it was a reasonable interpretation of our Constitution, one with which many experts agreed.

Following the Dobbs decision, activists repeatedly protested in front of the homes of many of the Justices, interfering with their lives, and likely making them feel personally unsafe. One armed protestor threatened the life of Justice Kavanaugh. Though the right to protest is fundamental, there are legal limits, and it is likely the protestors broke both Federal and State laws. The Justices and judges deserve security as they carry out their jobs.

I understood most of it when I read it again, in my 50s, the mother of three teens. With brilliant writing, unmistakeable characters, great dialogue (inner and spoken), deeply touching themes, it deserves all the praise it gets, and yes, it's a mystery that JDS character has escaped the criticism (justified IMO) of his relationships with teens.

And this isn't the only issue, particularly nationally, where Americans consistently say they want X but the government doesn't do that. Money in politics, at a minimum, has warped incentives on who's worth listening to.

That is not how a small-d-democratic government is meant to work. And I think people are getting fed up with feeling like our representatives - the people who work for us - are in it for themselves.

Don’t those opposed to data centers realize that the costs for everyone using data will increase as data demand confronts a data center shortage? This shortage is making data more costly for essential services like hospitals, police, infrastructure like water treatment plants, as well as academic and medical research and national security.

I use AI services dependent on data centers for my work and have noticed an increase in rates recently in part due to a shortage of data centers for processing. I can pay the higher rates because AI is essential for my work. But many cannot and will have to cut back on data use or encounter rationing of data.

Maybe that’s possible. If people opposed to data centers could restrict their use of cell phones by turning off cellular data options, stop backing up data in the cloud, turn off cybersecurity updates, avoid non-essential emailing, cancel their social media accounts and stop streaming videos on Netflix and YouTube, we can reserve the data centers for essential work. This would help keep costs down and slow the need for new data centers.

Although Peter Navarro might be the worst economist the US has produced in generations, he is right about the ability of the US and the world to diversify away from Chinese rare earths.

What Peter Navarro gets very wrong, although not mentioned much in this piece, is his insistence this must happen domestically.  There is a good case for the US to develop rare earth mining and refining for defense purposes, but the real solution is for rare earth mining and refining be developed globally to diversify sources to have healthy and diverse global competition and where absolute and comparative advantage can be harnessed to its fullest.

It is really important to remember something about rare earths:

Despite their name, rare earth minerals are not geologically rare at all. 

These are minerals that can be found in almost every part of the world and that means a lot of developing nations can and should play a role in diversification of sources for these minerals and a way to keep these minerals low cost for greater economic use.

If we, along with other developed nations and economies, can help usher in the wide diversification of mining and refining of rare earths globally - we remove the ability of China to control supply while ensuring the low cost of these critical minerals for our economy and the global economy.

But there are other epidemiologic lines of inquiry; specifically I'm recalling how John Snow, a physician in early industrial London, 1854, used the geography of cholera cases to identify the feces encrusted wooden water pump as the problem. He pulled out the water pump and cholera cases dropped. 

So why not map the location of cyclospira cases to search for clusters and then check for the parasite on local sources of produce. 

And why not say out loud, it is not the raw produce but the fecal contamination on produce that is the problem. In this sense, we have not come so far from the lack of sanitation of 1894 London where fecal contamination was not controlled; in our very complex, advanced food supply, we are still sickened by feces contaminated produce.

Produce is a major problem to keep free of pathogenic agents.   Most of what we think about is bacterial such as Listeria monocytogenes or various species of Salmonella.    Cyclosporiasis and another parasite, Cryptosporidium among other single cell parasites can also be ingested from produce.

There is no ability to keep agents free of contamination and washing berries and some other produce agents markedly impairs their potential for proper survival of storage and transfer.   Raspberries in particular, a major focus of Cyclospora carriage needs handles rinsing poorly unless done very shortly before its use.

Parties can use Chlorine gas to inactivate oocysts of the parasites. the analogs of the 'fruiting bodies' of these parasites.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0956713525003196 -refers to Cryptosporidium, but also works for Cyclospora as well.

More practical, but unacceptable is flash irradiation of produce.

Gamma irradiation has no capacity to alter the fruit's genetic contents to any significant extent as the genetics are already expressed as the present phenotype, the fruit itself being fully developed.  So long as the fruit is not planted after irradiation, there is no risk.   For vegetables there is no genetic worth to damage which will later change as no further development is possible.

Radiation also controls insect infestation.
https://wikifarmer.com/library/en/article/irradiation-technologies-in-vegetable-and-fruit-storage

It would serve the party well to place greater emphasis on those issues.

I also wish we had real debates instead of highly scripted television events. comments.name: Ayn Rant
comments.body:
In discussing China, keep in mind these peculiarities

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is neither Communist nor a political party, but it is historically and uniquely Chinese. Communism was tried in the Mao reign. It failed and was expunged. Only the name remains. Politicians and political parties are banned in China as nuisances that promote confusion and division and impede consensus and decision. 

The traditional  Chinese government form developed over several dynasties and many centuries. It consists of a figurehead Emperor or President, guided by a prestigious and persuasive body of advisors and administrators who are selected by merit and competitive examination. President Xi and the the CCP are the modern counterparts. 

The Chinese public does not participate in policy formation. Public satisfaction with government policy is based on demonstrable achievements.

EMTs and Paramedics in the FDNY are, however, not sworn. Despite a NY court order forcing the city to negotiate with the EMS union as if it were an essential service provider, the fact that EMS is 4 years out of contract shows how useless that ruling is. 

Also the fact that unlike the 4 essential services, FDNY EMS has to work 30 years for a 70% pension whereas cops and fire get 50% percent pension in 20 years. The very strong IFFA has told every member department in North America to absorb EMS units to prevent a collapse of the fire service. Some fire chiefs I work with in IL work at extremely well-paid departments and can't keep younger firefighters in the system because 95-97% of the department's work is ambulance work.

911 ambulance system collapse nationwide is coming...

I am not sure of the importance of these findings. It is already known that almost all Alzheimer’s victims have amyloids in their brains, shown from their autopsies. Many people with no signs of Alzheimer’s, however, also have amyloids in their brains, shown from their autopsies.

Currently, the only FDA approved drugs for Alzheimer’s are the amyloid-removal drugs Lecanemab and Donanemab. These have mild efficacy and significant side effects, including risk of brain swelling and bleeding. They are thought to delay, not halt, further declines in patients with diagnosed Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI).

This is not said to disparage these important amyloid-removal drugs. There are other Alzheimer’s drugs in the pipeline, meaning that even a delay in cognitive decline can help in the long run. It is essential, however, to understand that because of their side effects, cost, and limited efficacy, these amyloid-removal drugs are generally NOT given as a preventative measure if the only symptoms are amyloid in the blood. Patients must also have MCI, and negative tests for other factors (such as low B-12) that can cause MCI, to become candidates for amyloid-removal drugs.

The p-tau217 blood test is a useful diagnostic tool for initial amyloid screening of patients over 55 presenting with MCI, which is currently its FDA approved use. I’m not sure it is at all helpful for younger people without MCI. It might instead cause them worry about a condition they may never develop.

My current cognitive testing would have looked normal.

I reviewed the screening available.  Individually, ghey were not very sensitive.  They also were not very specific.  There were many false positives.

One article a year ago claimed  in the aggregate. The tests wiuld give high sensitivity and selectivity.  

But one group in the study had dementia.  The other group showed early cognitive decline.  Not helpful

I confirmed my impressions with a a neuroscientist.  Current  tests are not useful for most people in planning life decisions.

This or that newly "approved" med will delay, change, improve, slow progress, blah, blah, blah. It's plaque, no it's not. It's Alzheimer's, oh maybe it's mixed dementia. Diet, exercise, etc., on and on and on. In fact, there is no current protocol that treats dementia in any significant way. I can promise you that no amount of vitamins, kale and yoga will alter the progression. 

Now the focus is on finding out whether one is at risk? And what exactly would be the point in that? Splurge on that round the world cruise, make sure you have power of attorney, DNRs, in place? Live (who knows how long) with a 100 lb. anvil hanging over your head without any possibility of escaping it? 
There is no mention in this piece about the caretakers. First with my mother, then father, I entered the fun house horror ride of years of non-stop, pre-death grieving and putting my own life on hold, the wild west of hiring caregivers, the terrifying drainage of resources, financial and otherwise, the incredibly opaque and depressing option of euphemistically named "memory care facilities, and the so-called respite of hospice care. Let's be crystal clear about what dementia is and is not, what one can expect, and let's have medical professionals, including Drs., big Pharma, scientists, and insurance companies step up with unvarnished honesty.

But neither guarantees that you will develop Alzheimer’s or heart blockage respectively. As time went on, we developed additional tests such as LDL, HDL, and Lpa to understand how cholesterol affects your risk and now plug these into risk equations including other factors before we treat. It was similar with the development of blood tests for a heart attack. This story will continue to evolve.

comments.name: Ferdinand
comments.body:
"American consumers got some relief in June after months of soaring prices."
That opening sentence is almost as misleading as the inflation graph itself.

There is no real "relief" when prices continue to rise. Inflation has slowed, but prices have not fallen. Consumers are simply paying more at a slower rate.

Consumers got some relief from the pace of price increases, but not from high prices themselves. 

Consider a product that cost $100 before the inflation surge. After 9% inflation, it costs $109. If inflation then falls to 4%, the price does not return to $100. It rises again to $113.36. At 3% inflation the following year, it becomes $116.76. Inflation is cumulative because each year's increase is applied to an already higher price.

Excluding food and energy from the "core" inflation measure may be useful for economists studying underlying trends, but it does little to reflect what consumers actually experience. Families do not exclude groceries or gasoline from their budgets, so those costs remain central to their cost of living.

Finally, this reporting assumes the government's inflation data are beyond question. Healthy skepticism toward official statistics should not be dismissed, particularly when confidence in public institutions has become increasingly polarized.

The New York Times can do better.

comments.name: Jaganathan
comments.body: "While global observers view China’s endless military and political purges as proof of Xi Jinping’s absolute control, the reality inside the compound of Zhongnanhai is likely far more insidious. In a system where dynastic succession is impossible, the remaining members of the Political Bureau are playing a sophisticated, long-distance shadow game. Operating through deniable proxies and weaponizing a 'coded script' of anti-corruption data, these sub-factions do not need to launch an overt coup. Instead, they subtly feed the leader’s inherent paranoia, using Xi himself as the ultimate instrument to flush out their rivals. By manipulating the purge from the shadows, the ultimate survivor isn't trying to overthrow the king—they are simply ensuring they are the only option left standing when the throne inevitably becomes vacant. They keep their operational leverage purely internal, immune to Western leaks—there are no Chinese names in the Epstein files, just think about it."

At busy times, we have to staff someone just to (repeatedly and politely, for hours on end) notify people at the front of the line that someone is ready and waiting to help them because they are looking at their phone or absorbed in conversation.

Standing in line at the Frick museum, I had the nicest chat with those waiting with me. But the most extraordinary queue had been waiting fully nine hours for the MoMa exhibition in the New National Gallery in Berlin, 2004, long before online tickets came along. 
Around ten people around me formed a firm group, talking along, keeping the line while we went to dinner or even took a break and had a look at the nearby Gemälde Gallery one after the other, all the while inching around the beautiful Mies-vander-Rohe-building. Time flew. 
I wouldn't want to repeat it, but it is a wonderful memory!

Who they are with? - and how interesting it is for everyone. Just don't push it! If folks signal a desire to keep to themselves, leave them to be.

comments.name: Kat
comments.body: I also find it helpful to think of it as a dedicated moment for mindfulness and meditation. Try spending a moment focusing on each of your senses ("What do I smell? What do I hear? What do I see?") or just seeing what happens if you let your mind veg out and drift for just 10 minutes of standing meditation. Looking at the wait as a gift to enjoy rather than something to suffer through really does help. I say this as someone who forgoes the Lightning Lanes at Disney world!

comments.name: Kat Galore
comments.body: Waiting in the security line for the Austin City Limits Festival, which I attend most years, I like to chat with the people around me. It's a good way to get suggestions for which shows to see and most people are in a good mood and ready for a fun day (even though it can be hot and humid and sometimes the staff aren't feeling so jolly). The same can be true for almost any line: At the airport, where are you going? At a museum, what are you most excited to see? Etc. Of course, you should try to pick up on the social cues of others -- some won't want to talk -- but it can be a nice way to pass the time and maybe learn something.

comments.name: Jay E. Simkin
comments.body:
President Xi Jinping has made China the World's largest prison. Central London may have more cameras per square kilometer than does Beijing, But China's public surveillance system is nationwide and - key point follows - officials' access to video is assured. 

This in-depth surveillance is rooted in the paranoia that is at the heart of China's Communist Party. The "masses" cannot be trusted to know what's best for them, so are easily led astray. Only Communists know what's best and how that can be achieved. 

This mistrust is rooted in an infinitely deep xenophobia, which in grounded in the bitter oppression of Chinese by foreigners from 1839-1949. Britain forced China to import opium grown in India, to offset Britons' huge demand for China's products (tea, silk, porcelain, etc.). China retaliates by fostering Mexican drug thugs' production of fentanyl - a very toxic opoid - and its exports to the U.S.

Japan was especially brutal. During the 1930s, Japan set up in China a biological warfare research unit. Weapons - e.g., bubonic plague - were tested on humans and used against non-combatant Chinese civilians.

China's Communists ended these abuses. But those abuses are as fresh as if they had occurred yesterday.

In sum, no one should visit China - or even take flights that if diverted, would land where flies China's flag - without the most compelling of reasons. Mr. Xi can at any time decided he needs a "bargaining chip". A visitor, who has broken no law, may be seized.

While it may be true that many Western journalists try to maintain a neutral stance when reporting on China, there is always an implicit bias due to cultural and ideological differences.  Such biases are often exploited by Western elites to shape a narrative beneficial to their causes.  The best example is this current case, when a NYT report got her visa cancelled because of Chinese government censorship (since the Western media is always righteous and moral), but all Confucius Institutes in the West (esp. in the US) are really organs of propaganda for the Chinese Communist Party and should therefore be banned.

The max injected dose of Wegovy (semaglutide) is 7.2mg/week.   For simple math, we'll call that 1mg/day.

The max pill dose is 25mg/day.

25mg pill is 300/mo.  750mgs for 300 dollars, or about .50c/mg.

7.2mg injection is 399/mo.   29mgs for 400 dollars, or about 13c/mg.

Same exact chemical from the same manufacturer, close to a 30X swing in price.   Sure, that makes perfect sense, right?

comments.name: noplanetb
comments.body:
Before becoming a wildlife conservationist with a focus on zoonotic diseases, I was, from childhood, a recorder player, mostly playing Renaissance and Baroque works.
My recorders were from flute makers in Germany from local pear wood; but the more I delved into the historically informed performances practices, the more I'd want baroque ones, with ivory.
Naturally, even as a teen, I didn't want elephants killed for ivory, but woodwind makers had a solution - just use mammoth ivory!
However, I discovered that most mammoth ivory is mislabelled elephant ivory, as illicit traders frequently disguise poached elephant tusks as mammoth to bypass bans.
And the trade acts as a huge laundering loophole, because wildlife traffickers mix illegal elephant ivory into legal shipments of mammoth tusks, knowing that customs and buyers struggle to tell the difference.
This was a major catalyst that made me aware of the wildlife trade, poaching, deforestation, and unfortunately, those who cherish the higher arts are some of the folks creating the demand for it, from Pernambuco to forest elephant ivory, legal (!) in Japan, for Hanko seals, plectrums (bachi) for the shamisen, biwa, koto, although forest elephants are severely threatened and populations reduced by 90%.
This isn't acceptable for me.
Classical music can't contribute to the wildlife trade, and if exotic woods must absolutely be used, they should be checked and double-checked to not come from deforestation, but reforestation projects.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:

Except for the black marketers, and those who buy from them, there are no bad guys here.
Continuing to innovate solutions, and negotiate among the parties, is the only way to approach solutions in situations like this.
A lot better than denying the importance of protecting of other species.
Regarding the plantation alternative, it may have a place. But it does little to protect ecosystems, unless there’s a creative solution for that, too.

comments.name: Bill Atwood
comments.body: Rodney Mohr, who was interviewed in the article spent a decade developing a bamboo bow which he could make en mass.   Players find these NuBows to be easily as good or better than the best carbon fiber bows and they are made exclusively from renewable materials.   While artificial materials such as carbon fiber can be made to have similar physical properties to wood,  the area where they come up short is internal damping.  They tend to over resonate.   I have a steel bow made a century ago which was sold by Sears among others.  It’s almost unplayable - it singings as you play; most annoying!  I have sold many of Mohr’s NuBows to local string players,  some of whom prefer them to their traditional bows.

comments.name: FAW
comments.body: I write not as an instrument maker or a player but as a woodworker. Many woods are prized for their qualities. Teak and mahogany and other tropical woods are prized not only for their beauty but for the moisture resistance, workability and insect resistance. Boat builders have found substitutes but the replacements are never as good. Some say the reason Stradivarius violins are so valuable is their wood and craftsmanship is gone. Once a wood is found to be well suited for a particular use, it is always in danger of being loved to death. As soon as the supply of a particular wood becomes restricted, the more valuable it becomes and the more it becomes the object of criminals. I find it difficult to justify seizing wood that has already been made into objects as well as wood that is already harvested. We need sensible regulations that treat all wood as precious. It is good to have this conversation.

comments.name: Margaret Melville
comments.body: I spent 25 years as a luthier. Rehaired bows, restored violins and know well the controversy surrounding these materials. Ivory bow head plates have been replaced with plastic or bone and you can get plastic tortoise shell. My husband and I worked at a bow shop in Chicago and my husband made the frogs and buttons from precious materials. It's good these materials have been replaced. Pernambuco has always been the ideal bow wood for its beauty, strength and flexibility and know bow makers have been involved in conservancy of the trees. Political authority tied to territorial borders actually is a relatively new invention in human history. The Treaties of Westphalia which came at the conclusion of the Thirty Years War (1618–1648) is widely cited as one of the main turning points in the development of territorial sovereignty as the main organizing principle of contemporary international affairs.

comments.name: Ignacio Götz
comments.body: Mr. Howard, you never answer your own question, what makes a good -- even a great -- goalkeeper? I'll tell you. I played goalie in Venezuela, beginning in 1946, then in Spain, briefly, and then for an extended period, semi-professionally, in India, from 1951 till 1963. I was trained by Gulielmo Mari, ex-player for the National Italian Team, and he taught me techniques copied from the star playing of Vacca, legendary Argentinian keeper. We studied the photos -- no videos, then, and from his example, Mari derived techniques of goalkeeping I practiced assiduously and learned to perfection. What makes a good keeper? Technique. Today, most keepers have none, and they rely on athleticism, which is useful, but not sufficient. The US keeper demonstrated this: he blundered for lack of technique. On the other hand, the Norwegian keeper shone for an abundance of solid technique, including daring to actually grab the ball, which for some unearthly reason most keepers today have forgotten how to do -- proof? Again, the US goalkeeper. Every technique I was taught was designed to shorten the time it takes to jump, and to be able to see the ball better because you are crouching, which also helps you to jump more quickly. All such techniques are empirically demonstrable, and if they are not taught it is because they are not known. Artists train at their tasks, and playing soccer is and artistic endeavor, and the skills must be learned.

While there will be many who will bash Warsh only because he's the Fed chair and they want to abolish the Fed , I was encouraged by Warsh's testimony today. He clearly indicated that the Fed's goal was controlling inflation and maintaining strong employment markets, and was not going to be influenced by Trump if he calls publicly for lower short rates.  While many will complain about the reality of the reported inflation numbers (which the Fed doesn't calculate) , Warsh made clear that he wants to improve the data and processes the Fed relies on to manage short term rates. He talked about how one goal is to make "unsticky" higher sticky prices that markets get used to. While he didn't explicitly say how he would look to get inflation down, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to know that keeping rates at current levels or enacting a slight rise would be the main weapon. 

I also like how he didn't take the bait from some of the members who were asking how the Fed would handle issues like farm costs, housing costs , minority unemployment etc - correctly noting that the Fed can't solve those problems, rather it's the members asking the questions that should be enacting solutions .

All in all, after only 6 weeks on the job, I think we have a solid Fed Chair that will do the right things for long term price stability which will benefit all citizens.

Wall Street wants an independent Fed, and this Court takes its cues primarily from the financial moguls. It will cater to Trump only when his agenda conforms to oligarchical priorities. While the FTC is a gadfly often hostile to corporate interests, the Fed keeps the economic ship afloat and on course in choppy waters. That's the difference.

This doesn't mean that Warsh isn't a political opportunist, just that the landscape is changing and Warsh is smart enough to follow the bouncing ball.  Warsh is a competent economist and neither an ideologue nor a lunatic. That puts him in the upper echelon of Trump World. And, unlike his fellow Trump appointees, he plans to be around long after his benefactor implodes.

How much of this is "gentlemen politics?" Does Powell really believe Warsh is good for the Fed? If Powell does not think Warsh is good for the Fed, the time to speak up was before the vote in Congress. comments.name: Jorge
comments.body:
Although the left wing media is always pounding the table for Fed "independence," an ephemeral atate of administrative existence that every president has tested, let's sing how loudly the left defends Kevin Warsh's "independence" if he follosw through and begins to lower rates, as Trump wants.

I bet the criticisms and accusations of Trump control will ring loud, without irony or historical context.

Why is it OK for wacko Democrats in Congress to attack Warsh and try to bend the Fed to their favored policies, if the President was barred from doing the same to his predecessor?

Fed independence is a myth.  Consider recent history:

Truman pressured the Fed (initially under Chair Thomas B. McCabe, later William McChesney Martin) to keep interest rates low during and after WWII.

Johnson summoned Martin to his Texas ranch, physically shoved him against a wall, and berated him: “Martin, my boys are dying in Vietnam, and you won’t print the money I need.” 

The White House Tapes capture Nixon urging Burns to “goose” the economy, with threats including packing the Fed board or curbing its independence.  Burns initially resisted but eventually eased policy.

 Chief of Staff James Baker told Volcker that “the president (Reagan) is ordering you not to raise interest rates before the [1984] election.” 

And Barack Obama did not need to pressure his chairman, Janet Yellen, whose "hot money" policies -- low rates and asset purchases -- aligned perfectly with Obama's political needs.

comments.name: A matter of Innuendos
comments.body: The problem for Bloomberg is that it is an American news organisation that doesn't understand English laws. A similar news organisation in Singapore, Mothership, printed the same story about the sale months before Bloomberg did and didn't a libel suit from the ministers. Why? Because their article was factual. Bloomberg recycled an old story into a new one about money laundering and sale of bungalows by wealthy people. The article reeks with innuendos, which as the trial shows, look intended. Innuedos, under English laws, are potentially defamatory. Not only was Bloomberg unable to prove that the ministers' deals were shady, they also got facts about caveats and disclosures wrong. In an age of anti-money laundering enforcement by regulators around the world, did they seriously think the Singapore government had no clue who is buying or selling multi-million dollar properties? Developers here can't even sell a $2 million condo without submitting all kinds of AML information.

comments.name: Leto
comments.body: In the US, news reporting is not merely about reporting facts, but spinning a narrative around facts. This is done through how the facts are selected and presented, what language is chosen. It’s this narrative that is the problem in Singapore. Personally I think this narrative spinning is the source of political polarisation in the US, because it makes news political. The reporters can claim that it’s all based on facts, but the readers can clearly sense the narrative spinning behind it, which destroys their trust in the reporting if they don’t agree with the reporters’s narrative. When such narratives are directed at foreign countries like China or Singapore, nobody in the US will complain. But when it’s directed at targets at home, it causes political polarisation. For a big country like the US, it can survive the polarisation and erosion of trust. But a small country like Singapore cannot, which is why Singapore takes a much tougher approach towards narrative spinning in news coverage about events in Singapore.

comments.name: MCM
comments.body:
The facts of the case were not in dispute. What apparently caused the problems for Bloomberg was the use of terms such as "cloaking" and "shrouded", which suggested that there was wrongdoing. This could be categorized as editorializing, the purpose being to guide the reader towards an impression which the authors wanted to create.
Some may think this is acceptable. And we see this done on a daily basis here. But those who think that it is the role of media to report facts, along with unbiased analysis, but not to tell readers how they should interpret these facts, will disagree.

comments.name: John R. Ross
comments.body:
The Bx12 Select Bus Service on Fordham Road is a textbook case of infrastructure that fails to deliver. Dedicated lanes are already in place, yet the route remains among the slowest in the Bronx—strangled by routine violations, weak enforcement, and mixed traffic that treats bus priority as optional. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s push to secure these lanes and keep them open is the correct first step. But lane enforcement alone will not solve the deeper connectivity crisis facing Bronx riders.

What requires priority attention is direct, reliable bus access from the Bronx to LaGuardia Airport. The current lack of streamlined service forces unnecessary transfers that waste time and erode reliability for airport workers, travelers, and connecting passengers. A ride on the BxM7 makes the operational case clear: a limited-stop bus serving the Hunts Point vicinity is feasible and would tap into real demand patterns without requiring entirely new infrastructure.

The improvements to the Bruckner Expressway present a strategic opening to expand both local and express bus service. By integrating strong bus priority into those upgrades and establishing new direct links from the 96th Street and Second Avenue corridor in Manhattan (Q train station) into the Bronx, we can finally deliver faster, more dependable connections where they are needed most—serving working communities and critical economic hubs without compromise.

comments.name: BDR50
comments.body:
I've been involved with IT my entire life, I'm not convinced that AI has wide applicability.

AI has niche positions where it does well, e.g., voice recognition, highly structured math, Target identification for the military, running a predictable system, e.g., a railroad, activities like chess, etc., that are rule based. Running CNC machinery is one.

The key here is that the AI model can be trained to do a specific task that is basically the same or similar each time.

On the other side of the coin:

AI does much more poorly the more that judgement and impressions come into play, e.g., customer service. When is the last time that a customer service AI bot actually solved your problem? You almost always end up going to a human for resolution because the bots can't understand your problem.

It is horrible at figuring out what people need except in very straightforward situations.

Keep in mind that an AI bot is trained to be good at a small number of things, and no bot is good at everything.

Just like you can't pick any human off the street when you need a relatively complex job done, e.g., Math, engineering, chemistry, medicine, Psychology, even Waymo.  That human needs some specific training.

The idea that AI can replace human programmers is a joke.

People pick a job they need done and then pick an AI bot to do it, which is opposite how it should be done. That bot may do that job very poorly.

You pick the bot first, see what it does well, and then use it for that.

Secretary Lonnie Bunch’s defiance highlights the resistance: an institution that should unite the public instead advances narrow ideological agendas.Americans are tired of it. Public funding requires balance and accountability, not activism. Efforts to reshape the Board of Regents represent a needed course correction. This isn’t a short-term political fight — it’s the beginning of a long-term project to stop the left from defining America and its history in their political image. The Smithsonian’s credibility depends on telling the full story: triumphs, struggles, and exceptionalism included. True independence means serving the broad public, not catering to elite academic fashions. Reform is overdue.

The last place that I lived in California was in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada near Yosemite National Park, I lived there from around 2017-2021. And we loved to backpack in the high Sierra.

But you more and more had to change outdoor plans when the wind shifted and turned the sky hazy or orange. Day time temperatures in the summer would often exceed 100F, it was a dry heat, but still hot. 

We used an evaporative cooler to cool the house, these work in dry climates by sucking a lot of air into the house through wet membranes that use evaporation to cool the air. Evaporative coolers use less energy than air conditioning and add humidity to the very dry air, an added benefit. We could get the house down to the high 70s on hot days (over 100F degrees  or 38C.)

But we started experiencing more and more wildfire smoke. You could not operate the cooler when the wind brought the smoke to your town. And when it’s really hot outside that becomes a problem.

Neighbors wells started going dry and they started getting letters from their insurance agencies, that they were being dropped due to wildfire risk. We had a good well, but the last year we were there our home insurance jumped from around $2,500/year to over $4,000.

We saw the writing on the wall. You may get a few years here and there of some relief but the trend decade to decade is hotter, more extreme drought, more extreme wildfire behavior.

The 2023 Canadian wildfires released more CO2 than the rest of Canadian sources combined (37 million acres burned). Climate models did not project fires like that until much later this century.

And recently this paper reported that the permafrost region has shifted from an important carbon sink into a net emitter of greenhouse gases, CO2 and methane.

Some natural systems like forests and frozen soils which minimized some of the impacts of our atmospheric experiment with our only planet are changing from being our friends to our enemies.

It's misleading to see this entirely as a Big Tobacco issue or a flavours issue.

While it's true that Big Tobacco will benefit from the FDA's new enforcement policy, so will all other vape companies (Big Tobacco does not dominate the market).

And while it's true that flavoured products will benefit, that's because they make up the majority of the market anyway.

The more important issues driving the FDA's policy decision are, I suggest, two:

First, the prolonged criticism it has come under for delays in reviewing applications for marketing authorisation. This has led to a strange situation where the US market is largely composed of products that are technically illegal.

In effect what the FDA is now saying is that it will treat them AS IF they were legal, provided their manufacturers have shown good faith by taking the first steps on the road toward legality (applying for "premarket tobacco product authorisation").

Second, as the reporter mentions, the market is flooded with Chinese vapes. There is an obvious trade-war "made in America" context here, and the FDA's policy will tend to work in favour of American companies which have made some effort toward compliance.

The question is whether this is a Band-Aid applied to a situation embarrassing for the FDA (its inability to effectively conduct enforcement against  products that are nominally illegal yet openly sold) - or the precursor to a long-term policy that makes life easier for legitimate vape companies.

This is the fire weather described so well in the book Fire Weather: On the Front Lines of a Burning World. A 2023 book by Canadian-American journalist John Vaillant

The last straw for me, living in California, was standing five years ago on the roof my house, carefully watching a wildfire just two miles away, assessing the wind direction, to see if I needed to grab my two cats and emergency bag and high tail it out of there, and into a major traffic jam.

Spent some years backpacking and watching the forests starting to die and burn, seeing neighbors lose home insurance while their wells dried up and smelled the heavy smoke for days on end. Saw the refugees who lost their homes to wildfire move to our town (I would have set my sights further afield). One such couple was in their late 80s, they lost their house in the Camp Fire.

Something like a billion animals died in the "heat dome" that hit the Pacific Northwest a few summers ago, the mussels cooked on the beach.

And decade to decade warming for the near term is virtually locked in. We can't procrastinate any longer if we wish a chance at sustaining organized human life.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
Thanks for reporting on the wildfire situation in California. What worries me in particular about these fires is that they are turning our forests from important carbon sinks into net emitters of carbon dioxide (CO2, a greenhouse gas).

The 2023 Canadian wildfires released more CO2 than the rest of Canadian sources combined (37 million acres burned). Climate models did not project fires like that until much later this century.

And recently this paper reported that the permafrost region has shifted from an important carbon sink into a net emitter of greenhouse gases, CO2 and methane.

Some natural systems like forests and frozen soils which minimized some of the impacts of our atmospheric experiment with our only planet are changing from being our friends to our enemies.

I have been following Neko Health since shortly after its commercial launch in 2023. One early conversation with Daniel Ek still sticks with me. In response to a question about the company's profit outlook, he told me: “I would be super happy if this turned out to make me no money, but we actually solved real issues in the world for real people.”

It's a private company, and doesn't break out its finances. But investor interest is sky high, as today's funding announcement shows. Its valuation is nearly $7 billion even though it operates just eight clinics. That will soon change when it adds New York after the summer. 

The company faces challenges, for sure. The waiting list is huge, suggesting this kind of preventive scan will take time to scale. And every market they enter has prompted a wider debate about whether new tech like preventative scans can save lives.

The SAVE Act may or may not have good elements for voter registration and voting. (I tend to think it makes it difficult to vote, when the goal is to make voting fraud difficult). But it certainly is poorly timed.

The Act becomes effective immediately. And would almost certainly disenfranchise all military. And MANY others. The next election is 111 days away, and proof of citizenship IN PERSON is required. 

It seems like a small bit of prudence to always be making the election system more robust and more fraud-proof. But changes this close to an election can only lead problems.
